newsitem.title: USA: U.S. consumer credit unchanged in June.
newsitem.headline: U.S. consumer credit unchanged in June.

text.p: U.S. consumer installment credit was unchanged in June after rising a revised $2.5 billion at a 2.5 percent annual rate in May, the Federal Reserve said on Thursday.

It was the first month in more than four years that consumer credit failed to increase. Credit outstanding shrank in May 1993 by $700 million, but had risen in every month since then until leveiling out in June.
Wall Street economists had forecast that June consumer credit would rise by $5.2 billion.

Previously, the Fed said that May consumer credit had risen by $3 billion, but it revised that estimate down. Revised data to reflect updated seasonal factors, as well as modified procedures for reporting by finance companies was issued for the period from December 1990 onward.
In June, auto credit outstanding fell by $100 million at a 0.2 percent annual rate following a $100 million increase in May at a 0.4 percent rate.
Revolving, or credit-card credit, rose by $2.5 billion at a 5.8 percent annual rate in June, the Fed said. Credit-card debt had risen $1.7 billion at a 4.1 percent rate in May.

Other credit, which includes consumer bank loans like those for mobile homes and to pay for education, but not home equity loans or mortgages, fell $2.4 billion at a 9.5 percent annual rate in June. In May, this category of credit rose $600 million at an 2.5 percent annual rate.
The Fed said its revolving credit category has been expanded to include the revolving debt held by finance companies and the "other" category has been reduced by the same amount.
"Thus, this change does not affect total consumer credit," the Fed said. The seasonally adjusted total for all types of oustanding consumer credit in June was $1.217 trillion, the same as in May.
Before seasonal adjustment, total outstanding consumer credit in June was $1.211 trillion, up from $1.147 trillion a year earlier in June 1996.
